newsitem.title: USA: Eight charged in U.S. test-cheating scheme.
newsitem.headline: Eight charged in U.S. test-cheating scheme.

text.p: Eight people were indicted on Tuesday for an alleged scheme that let students cheat on graduate school admissions tests by using pencils secretly encoded with the answers.

The students, trained to read the code, used the pencils as they took the Graduate Record Exam (GRE), Graduate Management Admissions Test (GMAT) and Test of English as a Foreign Language (TOEFL), prosecutors said.
A 71-count indictment unsealed in Manhattan federal court charged Po Chieng Ma of Arcadia, California, and seven others with one count of conspiracy and 70 counts of mail fraud.

Under the scheme, expert test-takers would take the exams in New York City and, relying on the three-hour time difference, telephone the correct answers to Ma's Los Angeles office, the indictment claims.
In Los Angeles, the answers were quickly coded onto pencils and provided to graduate school applicants, it said.
Prosecutors would not disclose exactly how the answers were coded onto the pencils. "It's part of the evidence," said a spokesman for the U.S. Attorney's office in New York.
Students bought the test answers for fees ranging from $2,000 to $9,000, prosecutors said.
Charged with conspiracy in a separate complaint, also unsealed on Tuesday, were 12 students who allegedly used Ma's scheme to cheat on exams.
To participate, applicants were provided with sample test questions and answers so they could practice using the code, the complaint said.
According to the indictment, Ma and the others ran the cheating scam in almost every test date for the GMAT, GRE and TOEFL from June 1993 to October 1996.

The students equipped with the answers would take the tests at various sites around Los Angeles so their high scores would not be concentrated in one place and raise suspicion, the indictment alleged.
The scam was exposed when a test-taker became an informant, authorities said.

"The victims were not only the universities that accepted students who cheated ... but the honest students who may have been denied admission into the school of their choice because their place was taken by someone who cheated," said Mary Jo White, Manhattan U.S. Attorney.
If convicted, each defendant charged faces up to five years in prison on each charge and substantial fines.
Ma was first arrested in the case in October 1996 under the name George Kobayashi.
Also indicted was his wife, Chen Hui Chen, who along with another woman, Linda Chu Fan, is accused of writing the test answers on pencils and driving students to test sites.
